lead: Cloud security is a shared job. The provider protects the physical platform, the hypervisor and the network fabric. The customer protects identities, permissions, configurations, data and every exposed interface. An attacker needs one weak link: a reused password, a leaked API key, or a bucket policy set to public. This chapter defines threat, vulnerability, risk and attack vector. It maps common cloud attacks to the identity, network and storage layers. It uses the shared responsibility model to show why a provider control and a customer control must meet. You will use this map to review a cloud account or answer an exam question about a breach.
prereq: You need Unit 1's NIST cloud definition and service models, and Unit 2's web APIs and network basics.

sections.h3: Threat, vulnerability, risk and attack vector

blocks.text: Four words are often mixed. A threat is a possible cause of harm: a criminal, a worm, a careless employee. A vulnerability is a weakness that the threat can use: a weak password policy, an unpatched server, a bucket open to the internet. A risk is the chance and size of loss when a threat uses a vulnerability against an asset. An attack vector is the path or method used to reach the asset: a phishing email, a public API endpoint, a stolen key. Risk has two parts: likelihood and impact. In cloud work, the asset may be a bucket, a database, a VM or an identity. Exposure factor (EF) is the fraction of asset value lost in one incident. Single loss expectancy (SLE) is asset value × EF. Annual loss expectancy (ALE) is SLE × incidents per year. These numbers turn a vague fear into a budget question. If a bucket holds records worth ₹50,00,000 and one breach destroys 40% of that value, SLE is ₹20,00,000. Two incidents a year give ALE ₹40,00,000. The cloud attack surface is every interface a user, service or attacker can reach: consoles, APIs, SSH ports, bucket endpoints, IAM roles and third-party integrations. Each exposed interface must be authenticated, authorised, patched and monitored. The next section groups attacks by the layer they hit.
SLE = AV × EF;  ALE = SLE × λ
blocks.where: AV is asset value in rupees; EF is exposure factor, a fraction from 0 to 1; SLE is single loss expectancy in rupees; λ (lambda) is incidents per year; ALE is annual loss expectancy in rupees per year.

blocks.text: Credential theft hits the identity layer. Phishing, password reuse, leaked keys in code repositories and over-permissive roles let an attacker act as a valid user. MFA helps, but a stolen session token can bypass a password prompt. Short-lived credentials, least privilege and key rotation reduce this; see IAM and authentication. Misconfigured storage hits the storage layer. A bucket or blob container set to public read needs no exploit. Scanners find it. Missing logging is a second fault, so nobody sees the reads. Bucket policy, encryption and access logs are customer controls. Insecure APIs hit the network and application layer. A cloud is API-driven: every console click becomes a call. Missing input checks, weak tokens, exposed admin endpoints and no rate limit create paths. An API gateway with authentication, schema validation and throttling reduces this. DDoS hits availability. A flood of requests exhausts bandwidth, connection tables or application workers. Providers offer scrubbing and autoscaling, but a badly designed autoscale rule can raise cost. Co-residency hits isolation: two tenants share hardware, and a hypervisor or side-channel flaw may leak data. Providers patch hypervisors; customers patch guest OS and images. See VM security and secure isolation. Insider abuse comes from a provider or customer employee with legitimate access. Separation of duties, audit logs and least privilege limit it. Supply chain attacks enter through a compromised library, image, SaaS tool or provider, so you inherit their weakness. Signed images, software bills of materials and vendor review help. Map each vector to one layer for exam answers: identity for stolen keys, storage for public buckets, network for DDoS and APIs, isolation for co-residency, people and process for insider and supply chain.

sections.h3: Shared responsibility and the STRIDE checklist

blocks.text: The shared responsibility model splits controls. The provider is responsible for security of the cloud: physical sites, hardware, hypervisor, managed service code and the provider network. The customer is responsible for security in the cloud: identities, permissions, bucket policies, guest OS patches, data classification and application code. The split moves with the service model. In IaaS the customer patches the OS. In PaaS the provider patches the runtime, but the customer still protects code, secrets and data. In SaaS the provider runs the application, but the customer still manages users, sharing settings and data. The model is not a shield. A provider can pass every audit and a customer bucket can still be public. A customer can enable MFA and a provider API can still have a flaw. The meeting point is the interface: IAM policy, network rule, encryption key, API token. Test both sides there. STRIDE is a checklist, not a proof. It names six threat types: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege. Use it to ask one question per component: can an attacker pretend, alter, deny, read, block or escalate? It does not rank risk or find every cloud path. Pair it with the attack-path view and monitoring and incident response.

figure.caption: A stolen identity becomes a valid API key. The key reads a bucket whose policy grants read to any authenticated user, holding 10,000 records. The records leave as a breach. No single step is a provider platform break; each step is a customer-side control failure.

spec.title: One attack path
spec.aria: A four-step attack path from weak identity controls to a stolen key, a bucket policy that grants read to any authenticated user, and a data breach.

examples.question: A bucket policy grants read access to any authenticated user and holds 10,000 customer records. A stolen key provides that authenticated access. Asset value is ₹50,00,000, exposure factor is 0.4, and two such incidents happen a year. Find the single loss expectancy (SLE) and annual loss expectancy (ALE).
steps: Exposure factor EF = 0.4, so one incident loses 40% of asset value.
Incident frequency λ = 2 incidents per year.
examples.answer: SLE is ₹20,00,000 and ALE is ₹40,00,000 per year.
examples.check:
av = 5000000
ef = 0.4
incidents = 2
sle = av * ef
ale = sle * incidents
print(int(sle))
print(int(ale))

traps: A threat is not a risk. A threat is a possible cause of harm; risk combines likelihood and impact.
A vulnerability is not an attack. A public bucket is a weakness; a scanner reading it is the attack.
The provider secures physical hosts, but the customer still owns bucket policy, IAM and data classification.
A public bucket is usually a customer configuration error, not a provider platform breach.
DDoS damages availability, not confidentiality. Do not label it a data breach unless data was also read.

quiz.q: Define threat, vulnerability, risk and attack vector.
quiz.a: Threat: possible cause of harm. Vulnerability: weakness a threat can use. Risk: chance and size of loss. Attack vector: path or method used to reach an asset.

quiz.q: Why does shared responsibility not remove the customer's duty to secure a public bucket?
quiz.a: The provider secures the platform, but bucket policy, data classification and access settings are customer controls. A provider audit does not set or check every customer bucket policy.

quiz.q: Asset value is ₹80,00,000, exposure factor is 0.25, and three incidents happen a year. Find SLE and ALE.
A stolen API key reads a bucket whose policy grants read to any authenticated user. Map the attack to identity, storage and data layers.
quiz.a: Identity layer: weak credential control lets the key be stolen. Storage layer: over-permissive bucket policy grants read to any authenticated user, so the stolen key can read. Data layer: records are exfiltrated, causing a breach.

quiz.q: How is a DDoS attack different from a data breach?
quiz.a: DDoS attacks availability by exhausting resources. A data breach attacks confidentiality by reading or stealing data. A DDoS can hide a breach, but it is not the same event.

quiz.q: Name three cloud attack vectors covered in this chapter.
quiz.a: Any three: credential theft, misconfigured storage, insecure APIs, DDoS, co-residency, insider abuse, supply chain.

quiz.q: Why is STRIDE a checklist and not a risk proof?
quiz.a: STRIDE names six threat types and prompts questions per component. It does not rank likelihood or impact, and it does not expose every cloud-specific path, such as a server-side request forgery (SSRF) that reaches the instance metadata service or a confused-deputy trust policy on an IAM role.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry tools now combine cloud security posture management (CSPM) and cloud infrastructure entitlement management (CIEM) to find public buckets and risky roles automatically. Attack-path analysis joins identity, network and data findings into one graph, much like the figure. Zero-trust designs replace a trusted network with per-request checks of identity, device and context. Search for CSPM, CIEM, attack path analysis and the shared responsibility model.
